title: Singular value decomposition
summary: Every real m by n matrix factors as A=U Sigma V^T with U and V orthogonal and Sigma rectangular diagonal. The diagonal entries are nonnegative singular values, square roots of eigenvalues of A^T A, and the rank counts how many are nonzero. SVD is not the eigenvalue decomposition.
intuition:
The singular value decomposition is the factorization that exists for every real matrix, square or not. For $A$ of shape $m\times n$ it reads $A=U\Sigma V^\top$. The factor $U$ is an $m\times m$ orthogonal matrix, $V$ is an $n\times n$ orthogonal matrix, and $\Sigma$ is $m\times n$ and diagonal in the rectangular sense: the only nonzero entries sit at positions $(i,i)$, and those entries $\sigma_i$ are nonnegative. They are the singular values, usually written in nonincreasing order.

They come from an ordinary eigenvalue problem on a symmetric matrix. The product $A^\top A$ is $n\times n$, symmetric, and positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues are real and nonnegative. The singular values are the square roots of those eigenvalues. The columns of $V$ are orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^\top A$. For each positive $\sigma_i$ the corresponding column of $U$ is $Av_i/\sigma_i$, and the remaining columns of $U$ complete an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb{R}^m$. The rank of $A$ is exactly the number of nonzero singular values, because that is the number of positive eigenvalues of $A^\top A$, which has the same rank as $A$.

This is not the eigenvalue decomposition. Eigenvalues solve $Av=\lambda v$, so $A$ has to be square: $Av$ and $v$ live in the same space. A $3\times 2$ matrix has an SVD and does not have eigenvalues in that sense. Even for a square matrix the two diagonals differ. Singular values are nonnegative. Eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix can be negative, and the singular values are then the absolute values, not the eigenvalues themselves. A non-symmetric matrix can have all eigenvalues zero and still have a positive singular value, which is another way to see that $\Sigma$ is not $\Lambda$.

definitions.body: For any real $m\times n$ matrix $A$, an SVD is $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ with $U$ an $m\times m$ orthogonal matrix, $V$ an $n\times n$ orthogonal matrix, and $\Sigma$ an $m\times n$ rectangular diagonal matrix with nonnegative diagonal entries.

The singular values $\sigma_i$ are the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$. There are $n$ of them, counting multiplicity, and $\Sigma$ places them on its main diagonal, with extra zero rows if $m>n$ or extra zero columns if $n>m$.
The rank of $A$ equals the number of nonzero singular values. A zero singular value means a direction $v$ with $Av=0$.

formulas.name: SVD
formulas.note: $U$ and $V$ are orthogonal and $\Sigma$ is rectangular diagonal. The factorization exists for every real $m\times n$ matrix.

formulas.name: Singular values from $A^\top A$
formulas.note: The eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are nonnegative. The rank equals the number of nonzero singular values. These are not the eigenvalues of a non-square $A$, and they are not the eigenvalues of a square $A$ either unless that identification is justified.

properties: Every real $m\times n$ matrix has an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^\top$, with $U$ and $V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ rectangular diagonal and nonnegative on the diagonal.
Each singular value is the square root of an eigenvalue of the symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $A^\top A$.
$\mathrm{rank}(A)$ equals the number of nonzero singular values.
A rectangular matrix has an SVD. It does not have eigenvalues in the square-matrix sense, because $Av$ and $v$ live in spaces of different dimension.
SVD is not the eigenvalue decomposition. For a symmetric matrix the singular values are the absolute values of the eigenvalues. A negative eigenvalue does not appear as a negative singular value.

examples.title: SVD of a $3\times 2$ matrix
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find the singular values from $A^\top A$, and check a full SVD by multiplying $U\Sigma V^\top$ back to $A$.
steps: $A^\top A=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Its characteristic polynomial is $\lambda(\lambda-4)$, so the eigenvalues are $4$ and $0$. The singular values are $\sigma_1=\sqrt{4}=2$ and $\sigma_2=0$. One of them is nonzero, so $\mathrm{rank}(A)=1$.

An orthonormal eigenbasis of $A^\top A$ is $v_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1)^\top$ for eigenvalue $4$ and $v_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-1,1)^\top$ for eigenvalue $0$. Then $Av_1=\sqrt{2}\,(1,1,0)^\top$, so $u_1=Av_1/\sigma_1=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(1,1,0)^\top$. Extend by $u_2=\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(-1,1,0)^\top$ and $u_3=(0,0,1)^\top$.

With these columns, $\Sigma=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. The product $U\Sigma$ is $\bigl(\sqrt{2}\,(1,1,0)^\top,\ 0\bigr)$, and right-multiplication by $V^\top$ spreads that first column into the two equal columns of $A$. Numerically, $U\Sigma V^\top=A$. The sum of the squares of the singular values is $4+0=4$, which equals the sum of the squares of the entries of $A$.
examples.answer: The singular values are $2$ and $0$, the rank is $1$, and one SVD is the $U$, $\Sigma$, and $V$ above. The product $U\Sigma V^\top$ returns $A$.

examples.title: Singular values are not the eigenvalues
examples.prompt: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Find its eigenvalues and its singular values, and explain why a $3\times 2$ matrix can have one list and not the other.
steps: $A$ is symmetric and $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}$, while $A\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}=-\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}$. The eigenvalues are $1$ and $-1$.

$A^\top A=A^2=I$, whose eigenvalues are $1$ and $1$. The singular values are $\sqrt{1}$ and $\sqrt{1}$, that is $1$ and $1$. The negative eigenvalue became a positive singular value. An SVD can use $\Sigma=I$, which is not $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$.

A $3\times 2$ matrix maps $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$. There is no scalar $\lambda$ and nonzero $v\in\mathbb{R}^2$ with $Av=\lambda v$, because the two sides have different shapes. The same matrix still has a $3\times 3$ orthogonal $U$, a $2\times 2$ orthogonal $V$, and a $3\times 2$ matrix $\Sigma$.
examples.answer: The eigenvalues are $1$ and $-1$. The singular values are $1$ and $1$. Rectangular matrices have an SVD and do not have eigenvalues in the square sense.

traps: Calling the SVD the eigenvalue decomposition. For $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues are $1,-1$ and the singular values are $1,1$. The diagonal factor $\Sigma$ is not allowed to carry a negative entry.
Asking for the eigenvalues of a rectangular matrix. A $3\times 2$ matrix has two singular values and no square-matrix eigenvalues, because $Av$ and $v$ have different lengths.
Taking signed square roots. Singular values are nonnegative. The square root of an eigenvalue of $A^\top A$ means the nonnegative one.

Counting the rank as the number of singular values, including zeros. The rank is the number of nonzero singular values. A $3\times 2$ matrix of rank $1$ has singular values such as $2$ and $0$, and the zero still occupies a diagonal slot of $\Sigma$.
python:
def mul(A, B):
    n = len(B)
    return [[sum(A[i][k] * B[k][j] for k in range(n)) for j in range(len(B[0]))] for i in range(len(A))]

def T(A):
    return [list(row) for row in zip(*A)]

A = [[1, 1], [1, 1], [0, 0]]
ATA = mul(T(A), A)
assert ATA == [[2, 2], [2, 2]]
# eigenvalues 4 and 0; singular values 2 and 0; rank 1
assert ATA[0][0] + ATA[1][1] == 4
assert ATA[0][0] * ATA[1][1] - ATA[0][1] * ATA[1][0] == 0
s = 2 ** 0.5
V = [[1 / s, -1 / s], [1 / s, 1 / s]]
U = [[1 / s, -1 / s, 0], [1 / s, 1 / s, 0], [0, 0, 1]]
Sigma = [[2, 0], [0, 0], [0, 0]]
recon = mul(mul(U, Sigma), T(V))
assert all(abs(recon[i][j] - A[i][j]) < 1e-9 for i in range(3) for j in range(2))
Sym = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]
assert mul(Sym, Sym) == [[1, 0], [0, 1]]
print(2)

questions.stem: Every real $m\times n$ matrix $A$ has a factorization of which form?
options: $A=U\Sigma V^\top$ with $U$ and $V$ orthogonal and $\Sigma$ rectangular diagonal
$A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$ with $\Lambda$ the eigenvalues, for every shape
$A=LU$ with no row swaps, for every invertible square $A$
$Av=\lambda v$ for a nonzero $v$, even when $m\neq n$
questions.solution: The answer is **A**. The SVD exists for every real matrix, rectangular included: $U$ is $m\times m$ orthogonal, $V$ is $n\times n$ orthogonal, and $\Sigma$ is $m\times n$ with nonnegative diagonal entries. The symmetric eigenvalue factorization needs a real symmetric matrix. Unpermuted LU can fail for an invertible matrix. Eigenvalues need a square matrix.

questions.stem: The singular values of a real matrix $A$ are
options: the eigenvalues of $A$, for a matrix of any shape
the nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$
the diagonal entries of $A$, whether or not $A$ was factored
questions.solution: The answer is **B**. The matrix $A^\top A$ is symmetric and positive semidefinite, its eigenvalues are nonnegative, and the singular values are their nonnegative square roots. They are not the eigenvalues of a rectangular $A$, they are not read off the entries of $A$ before a factorization, and the convention keeps them nonnegative. A negative eigenvalue of a symmetric $A$ contributes its absolute value.

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
options: A rectangular real matrix has a singular value decomposition.
A rectangular real matrix has eigenvalues in the square-matrix sense.
The rank equals the number of nonzero singular values.
The singular value decomposition is the same factorization as $A=Q\Lambda Q^\top$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A and C**. Every real $m\times n$ matrix has an SVD, and the number of positive diagonal entries of $\Sigma$ is the rank. A rectangular matrix has no eigenvalues via $Av=\lambda v$, because the two sides have different shapes. The factorization $Q\Lambda Q^\top$ is the spectral theorem for a real symmetric matrix, and its diagonal can contain negative eigenvalues. That is not $\Sigma$.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$. Which of the following are true?
options: The singular values of $A$ are $1$ and $1$.
The singular values of $A$ are $1$ and $-1$.
questions.solution: The correct options are **A, B, and C**. The matrix swaps the two coordinates, with eigenvectors $(1,1)^\top$ and $(1,-1)^\top$ for eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$. Also $A^\top=A$ and $A^2=I$, so $A^\top A=I$ and both eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are $1$. The singular values are the nonnegative square roots, $1$ and $1$. A singular value is not negative, so D is false.

questions.stem: Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$. The eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are $4$ and $0$. Enter the sum of the singular values of $A$.
questions.solution: The answer is **2**. Singular values are nonnegative square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$, so they are $\sqrt{4}=2$ and $\sqrt{0}=0$. Their sum is $2$. The rank, which is the number of nonzero singular values, is $1$ rather than this sum.
